The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence is creating a major opportunity in the central processing unit (CPU) market, positioning Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD) for robust growth.
Bank of America strategists expect the server market to expand from approximately $61 billion to $211 billion by 2030. The firm estimates that roughly $180 billion of the $211 billion server CPU market in 2030 will be tied to AI workloads, creating a significant market for AMD’s EPYC server processors.
AMD also ranks among Insider Monkey’s 11 AI Stocks That Will Go to the Moon— but where does it rank among the other AI names on the list?
On September 25, the research firm reiterated a Buy rating on AMD. It raised its price target to $720 from $620, citing the company’s opportunity to capture a larger share of the rapidly expanding CPU market.
AMD’s rally has already pushed expectations sharply higher, raising a tougher question: what does a $1 trillion valuation now demand from AMD’s AI ambitions?
Agentic AI Could Boost Demand for AMD CPUs
BofA’s higher price target comes as the firm expects agentic AI to increase demand for CPUs that coordinate workloads, manage data, and support increasingly complex AI systems.
Rather than replacing GPUs, CPUs are increasingly complementing them within AI infrastructure. This trend is already supporting AMD’s CPU business.
The price target hike comes as BofA expects agentic AI to fuel demand for CPUs to coordinate workloads and manage data. CPUs increasingly complementing GPUs rather than competing with them drove growth in AMD CPU revenue in Q2. Client business revenue was up 23% year over year to $3.1 billion, driven by strong demand for Ryzen processors.
Additionally, Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. is well positioned to gain from AI infrastructure beyond GPUs. The company offers a wide range of platforms that combine EPYC CPUs with Instinct GPUs and networking technologies. That was one reason the company’s data center revenue rose 107% in the second quarter to $6.72 billion, driven by growth in EPYC server CPUs and Instinct GPUs.
AMD’s AI Opportunity Extends Beyond GPUs
BofA’s bullish view does not depend on Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. replacing Nvidia as the dominant provider of AI accelerators. Instead, the firm sees AMD as a potential beneficiary of the broader evolution of AI computing architecture.
As AI workloads become more complex and increasingly autonomous, data centers require CPUs, GPUs, networking, and other components to work together efficiently. This creates an opportunity for AMD to benefit from the overall expansion in AI infrastructure, even if GPUs remain the primary engines for many AI workloads.
The opportunity surrounding CPUs could become particularly important as agentic AI applications require greater coordination between different computing resources.
Advanced Micro Devices, Inc.’s rapid expansion in AI has also raised expectations for the stock. The stock has gained more than 180% in 2026, reflecting investor optimism about the company’s ability to capture a larger portion of the AI infrastructure market.
The stock trades at a premium, with a forward price-to-earnings multiple of 39X, roughly two times Nvidia’s 19X. This means investors are paying considerably more for each dollar of AMD’s expected future earnings.
Nevertheless, robust growth from a smaller base justifies AMD’s valuation, as second-quarter revenue was up 50% while data center revenue more than doubled year over year. On the other hand, Nvidia boasts of a profitability advantage, as its gross margins stand at about 75% compared to AMD’s 54%.
Any signs that AI infrastructure spending is slowing, or that AMD is capturing less of the expected CPU opportunity, could pressure investor sentiment. A significant portion of expected growth is also tied to hyperscalers, AI labs, and data-center infrastructure providers. If these customers reduce or delay capital expenditures, the company could experience a meaningful slowdown in growth.
Institutional investors have also been increasing their exposure to AMD amid the AI boom. As of the second quarter, 164 hedge funds held positions in AMD, up from 134 in the first quarter, indicating increased institutional participation.
Among individual investors, Marshall Wace LLP increased its AMD position by 3% to approximately $2.26 billion, while DE Shaw reduced its exposure by 21% to approximately $1.79 billion.
Short interest, meanwhile, remained relatively modest. AMD had approximately 39.98 million shares sold short as of September 15, down from 41.71 million shares on August 31. That represented approximately 2.46% of the float. That represented short interest of approximately 2.45%.
Advanced Micro Devices, Inc.’s investment story is increasingly tied to the broader AI computing ecosystem rather than GPUs alone. BofA’s $720 price target reflects the firm’s view that the rapid growth of AI workloads could create a substantial opportunity for AMD’s EPYC CPUs alongside its Instinct GPUs and networking products.
The key question for investors is whether the company can continue translating the enormous growth in AI infrastructure spending into sustained CPU and data-center revenue growth. With expectations already elevated following the stock’s substantial rally, execution, hyperscaler spending, and the pace of AI adoption will remain important factors for AMD shares.

AMD (AMD) Could Issue 320 Million Shares at a Penny. Here is What Has to Happen First
The Shares Only Arrive If the Chips Do:
A warrant is not a share until it vests, and these vest against deliveries. Each holder earns its tranches by buying AMD processors, up to six gigawatts of deployed capacity apiece. Nothing vests on the signing. So the dilution and the revenue arrive together. AMD only hands over the equity if the customer has already bought the hardware that justifies it.
The final OpenAI tranche carries one more condition: a $600 share price. AMD traded at $655.90 on October 6, so that threshold is already cleared. What this structure does is convert a customer into a shareholder at the pace the customer spends. Revenue grew 50.10% in the most recent quarter, which is the rate this arrangement is designed to extend.
Billionaire investors hold ten semiconductor stocks. The one ranked first has returned 24% since June.
What 320 Million Shares Would Actually Cost:
Dilution is the right worry, and its size depends on how it is measured. AMD is worth $1.07 trillion. At the current price, 320 million shares represent roughly $210 billion of value handed over for $3.2 million.
Against the market capitalization, that is close to a fifth of the company. The defense is that twelve gigawatts of processors between them is an enormous order, and the equity is the discount attached to it.
Whether that trade is a good one depends on a margin the vesting does not guarantee. Operating margin is 17.25% and net margin 15.58%, both modest for a company priced like this. The balance sheet is not the constraint. Debt of $4.28 billion against $13.11 billion of cash gives debt-to-equity of 6.36%.
We named ten stocks for the year ahead in October. What put the first one on top is explained here.
The Valuation Case:
AMD traded at around $656 on October 6 after rising 198.69% over twelve months. Sustainability is the question the warrants themselves ask, because they only pay off for AMD if these two buyers keep deploying at scale.
On price, almost nothing is cheap. The stock trades at 167.32 times trailing earnings and 41.72 times forward. Enterprise value to EBITDA of 106.93 is the figure that stands furthest from the business, since EBITDA of $9.56 billion is small against a trillion-dollar valuation.
A beta of 2.45 means these shares move more than twice as hard as the index. Short interest is only 2.46%, so the market is not positioned against the story.
Conclusion:
The warrants are better structured than the headline number suggests. Nothing vests without deliveries, so the 320 million shares only appear if six gigawatts of processors have been sold to each buyer. The $600 condition on the final tranche is already met at $655.90. However, at full vesting this is close to a fifth of the company for $3.2 million, and the operating margin funding it is 17.25%. At 167.32 times trailing earnings, the price assumes the orders arrive in full. The number to watch is deployed gigawatts, because that single figure decides both the revenue and the dilution.

Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD) was held by 164 hedge funds with a combined stake value of about $23.58 billion at the end of Q2 2026 in the Insider Monkey database. This is up from 134 hedge fund holders with a cumulative investment value of around $8.71 billion in the previous quarter.

In July 2026, Marvell signed an agreement with Google, a unit of Alphabet (GOOGL +0.35%), to develop custom chips, including AI inference accelerators.The race for AI infrastructure supremacy continues to reshape the market as investors weigh high-growth chipmakers. Choosing between Advanced Micro Devices (AMD +2.80%) and Marvell Technology (MRVL +5.81%) requires a close look at their recent performance and valuation.
Advanced Micro Devices has grown from a PC chipmaker into a company whose largest segment is data center chips. Marvell specializes in the cloud's networking and storage backbone. Both companies benefit from the massive shift toward artificial intelligence, but they address different layers of the semiconductor landscape, offering unique risk-reward profiles for your portfolio.
Advanced Micro Devices designs high-performance computing products for data centers, gaming consoles, and personal computers. Its Instinct line of accelerators competes directly in the artificial intelligence market, making it a key player among semiconductor stocks.
The company also supplies the custom chips inside the Xbox Series X and S consoles from Microsoft (MSFT +0.78%). Its annual report warns that it depends on a small number of customers for a substantial portion of its business, which adds a layer of risk.
In the fiscal year ended Dec. 27, 2025, revenue reached nearly $34.6 billion, up about 34.3% from the prior fiscal year. The company reported net income from continuing operations of roughly $4.3 billion during this period, a net margin of approximately 12.3%.
Those results absorbed about $440 million in net inventory and related charges tied to U.S. export controls on its MI308 chips for China. Data center revenue rose 32% on demand for EPYC server processors and Instinct GPUs. Client and gaming revenue grew 51%, and embedded revenue slipped 3%.
Based on total debt, the debt-to-equity ratio was about 0.05x as of Dec. 27, 2025, meaning the company had very little debt relative to its equity. AMD sold $4.75 billion of senior notes in August 2026 for general corporate purposes, which may include debt repayment, so its debt load has grown, though it remains small relative to its equity.
The current ratio was roughly 2.9x as of Dec. 27, 2025, which measures a company's ability to cover short-term debts with short-term assets. Free cash flow, a non-GAAP figure AMD calculates from the operating cash flow of continuing operations minus capital expenditures, was about $5.5 billion in the fiscal year ended Dec. 27, 2025.
Note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 25.2% of operating cash flow from continuing operations, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.
Investors should also weigh potential dilution. AMD has issued warrants for up to 160 million shares each to OpenAI and Meta Platforms (META -0.41%), together roughly a fifth of its current share count. As of June 27, 2026, none of those shares had vested.
They vest as each customer's GPU purchases hit set milestones, subject to other technical and commercial conditions. The warrants also include stock price thresholds that cap at $600 per share for the final tranche, a level AMD's stock already trades above. AMD also agreed in September 2026 to buy World Labs, an AI research lab led by Fei-Fei Li, in an all-stock deal valued at about $8.2 billion.
That purchase, expected to close by the end of 2026, would add more shares on top of the warrants, and Li would join AMD as chief scientist.
Marvell Technology operates as a fabless semiconductor firm, meaning it designs chips but outsources the actual manufacturing to partners. It focuses on data infrastructure solutions, particularly custom silicon and high-speed networking hardware for cloud providers. In July 2026, Marvell signed an agreement with Google, a unit of Alphabet (GOOGL +0.35%), to develop custom chips, including AI inference accelerators.
As part of the deal, Marvell issued Google a warrant in August for up to about 59 million shares, roughly 7% of its share count, that vests chiefly as Google's custom chip purchases grow. Customer concentration is a factor here, as the top 10 customers accounted for 82% of total net revenue in fiscal 2026.
In the fiscal year ended Jan. 31, 2026, revenue reached nearly $8.2 billion, up about 42.1% year over year, which management attributed to AI demand in its data center business. The company reported net income of roughly $2.7 billion, a net margin of approximately 32.6%, compared with a net loss in the prior fiscal year. That swing came largely from a one-time pre-tax gain of about $1.8 billion on the August 2025 sale of its automotive Ethernet business. GAAP operating margin, which excludes that gain, was about 16%.
Based on total debt, the debt-to-equity ratio was approximately 0.3x as of Jan. 31, 2026. Its current ratio was approximately 2.0x as of Jan. 31, 2026, indicating it has about twice the short-term assets needed to pay its current liabilities. Free cash flow for the fiscal year ended Jan. 31, 2026, was nearly $1.4 billion.
Stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 33.8% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation because SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.
Advanced Micro Devices faces intense competition from Intel (INTC -3.18%) and Nvidia (NVDA +0.14%), which can use their massive scale to pressure pricing. The company also faces significant geopolitical risks, particularly U.S. export controls on advanced chips to China.
Furthermore, relying on Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM -0.72%)for all of its processor and GPU wafers at 7 nanometers or smaller creates geographic concentration risk regarding potential regional disruptions.
Marvell Technology has a high revenue concentration, with one distributor accounting for about 37% of its fiscal 2026 net revenue. It also faces competitive pressure from Broadcom (AVGO +3.67%) and Qualcomm (QCOM +0.13%), as well as rivals like Nvidia and Intel.
Integrating Celestial AI and XConn Technologies, two acquisitions that closed in February 2026 after its fiscal year ended, and managing export controls are ongoing challenges that could affect future operational results.
Marvell carries the lower forward earnings multiple in the table below, and the two stocks trade at nearly identical sales multiples. The Forward P/E compares a stock price to future earnings estimates. The P/S ratio measures market value against sales over the past twelve months.
MetricAdvanced Micro DevicesMarvell Technology

Which stock would I buy in 2026?
I'd lean toward AMD, though its warrants tied to OpenAI and Meta carry costs for shareholders.
If every tranche vests, those warrants would add roughly a fifth to AMD's share count. AMD's stock already trades above the $600 price threshold set for the final tranche, so vesting now rests mainly on both customers scaling up their GPU purchases. That dilution comes paired with the growth AMD wants anyway.
What tips me toward AMD is breadth. It sells its own AI accelerators and server processors to major AI spenders, and its PC chip business continues to grow. Gaming has softened, and the data center now makes up more than half of revenue. Marvell's custom chip model ties its fortunes to a small group of cloud giants, and its 10 largest customers, including distributors, accounted for more than 80% of sales last fiscal year.
Its headline profit also benefited from a one-time gain from the sale of its automotive Ethernet business, so its underlying earnings power is thinner than the net margin suggests.
Neither stock is cheap after huge runs, and chip demand moves in cycles, so I'd expect sharp swings along the way. Marvell trades at a lower forward earnings multiple. For investors who plan to hold for five years or more and add shares gradually, I still think AMD's broader business is worth that premium. Investors who want more direct exposure to custom AI chips and can live with heavier customer concentration may prefer Marvell.

Su assumed the chief executive position on October 8, 2014. At that juncture, shares traded near $3 and the entire enterprise commanded a mere $2.5 billion market capitalization.
Cramer’s Focus: Central Processing Units Over Graphics Accelerators
Cramer’s bullish perspective on Advanced Micro Devices doesn’t center on graphics processing technology. Instead, he’s concentrating on central processing units and the emerging paradigm of agentic artificial intelligence.
Agentic AI architectures possess the capability to analyze situations, formulate strategies, and execute decisions autonomously. AMD’s EPYC server processor lineup has steadily captured market share from Intel over recent years. Data center segment revenue reached $6.7 billion during Q2 2026, representing a 107% year-over-year increase.

As the artificial intelligence boom matures, choosing between high-growth processors and steady analog chips requires a careful look at Advanced Micro Devices (AMD +2.80%) and Texas Instruments (TXN +0.79%) as potential long-term investments.
Advanced Micro Devices focuses on high-performance computing for data centers and gaming, while Texas Instruments dominates the analog world with chips for industrial and automotive uses. While both operate in the same broad category, their business models and growth profiles offer very different opportunities for retail investors today.
Advanced Micro Devices designs processors and graphics chips for everything from laptops to massive data centers. Key partnerships include a strategic agreement with OpenAI to deploy advanced graphics units, alongside long-term deals with Sony (SONY +1.32%) and Microsoft (MSFT +0.78%) for gaming hardware. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business since a few large buyers drive much of the volume.
In fiscal 2025, revenue reached nearly $34.6 billion, an increase of 34% over the prior year. Net income was roughly $4.3 billion, and AMD reported a net margin of approximately 12.5% for the year. This upward trend highlights the strong demand for the company's newest products among semiconductor stocks.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.1, indicating that AMD relies very little on borrowed money. The current ratio, which measures a company's ability to pay short-term debts with current assets, is roughly 2.9. Free cash flow reached nearly $6.7 billion, though note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 21.2% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.
Texas Instruments offers a massive catalog of more than 80,000 products, focusing on analog and embedded processing. The company serves over 100,000 customers globally, primarily in the industrial and automotive markets. Because the customer base is highly diverse, with roughly half of total revenue generated by customers outside of its largest 50, the company does not rely heavily on any single buyer.
In fiscal 2025, revenue reached nearly $17.7 billion, up 13% compared to the previous year. Net income was $5 billion, resulting in a net margin of roughly 28%. In its latest annual report, filed for the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, Texas Instruments highlighted its focus on making electronics more affordable through its manufacturing scale.
Based on the December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is close to 0.9. The current ratio is approximately 4.4, suggesting the company maintains a strong cushion for its immediate financial obligations. Free cash flow for the year was nearly $2.6 billion, providing capital to support its long-term manufacturing expansion and return value to shareholders.
Advanced Micro Devices faces intense competition from Intel (INTC -3.18%) and Nvidia (NVDA +0.14%), especially following strategic partnerships between those rivals. Geopolitical risks are also present, as U.S. export controls on advanced chips to China have caused inventory charges. Additionally, the company relies heavily on TSMC (TSM -0.72%) for manufacturing and must navigate the integration of recent acquisitions like ZT Systems.
Texas Instruments must manage the cyclical nature of the chip industry, which often sees volatile demand. Because the company owns its manufacturing plants, it faces high fixed costs that are difficult to reduce during market downturns. Significant revenue comes from customers in China, making it vulnerable to trade barriers. TI is also currently in the middle of acquiring Silicon Laboratories (SLAB -0.08%).
Advanced Micro Devices trades at a significantly higher premium than Texas Instruments when comparing the forward P/E and P/S ratio metrics.

Valuation metrics sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.
Which stock would I buy in 2026?
Presumably, investors are paying a premium for AMD because of its strong revenue growth (Texas Instruments' growth didn't come close to AMD's last fiscal year). That said, I am more interested in each company's net margin. Using fiscal 2025 figures, TI's margin pretty handily tops AMD's full-year results. And while both companies have seen profits expand by a few percentage points over the trailing 12 months, that profitability gap has continued into this fiscal year.
As far as their actual business models, I do think AMD's fabless approach is more attractive, because it gives the company more flexibility. Texas Instruments, conversely, has to deal with the high fixed costs of owning and running its manufacturing plants.
AMD stock has absolutely exploded over the past 10 years, while Texas Instruments shares have modestly outperformed the S&P 500 over that same time frame. Past performance is no indication of future results, but it's worth taking into consideration.
All told, I like Texas Instruments better here because it appeals to the conservative side of me: It’s not crazy expensive, it has stronger profitability, and it pays a dividend yielding just over 2.1%.

As the artificial intelligence boom shifts from cloud servers to edge devices, investors must decide which chip titan offers better value: Advanced Micro Devices (AMD +2.80%) or Qualcomm (QCOM +0.13%)?
Advanced Micro Devices has transformed itself from a secondary CPU maker into a powerhouse in data center GPUs and high-performance computing. Meanwhile, Qualcomm is leveraging its dominance in smartphone connectivity to expand into automotive systems and on-device AI. Both companies are vying for leadership in a rapidly evolving hardware landscape.
Advanced Micro Devices develops high-performance computing products for cloud infrastructure and gaming consoles. In its latest annual report, filed for the fiscal year ended December 27, 2025, the company highlighted a partnership with OpenAI and supply agreements with Microsoft (MSFT +0.78%). This customer concentration adds risk even as the firm expands among semiconductor stocks while integrating its new ZT Systems acquisition.
In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $34.6 billion, representing a significant growth of roughly 34.3% compared to the previous year. The company reported net income of approximately $4.3 billion and a net margin of roughly 12.5%. This trend suggests strong demand for its AI-focused hardware and server processors, which have become the primary engines of its financial performance as it gains market share.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio stands at roughly 2.9x, which is a metric that compares current assets to current liabilities to assess short-term liquidity. The debt-to-equity ratio, a measure of financial leverage, is approximately 0.1x. Free cash flow reached nearly $6.7 billion, though note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 21.2% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.
Qualcomm specializes in foundational wireless technologies and integrated circuits, primarily serving the mobile, automotive, and Internet of Things markets. Its latest annual report, filed for the period ending September 28, 2025, details a strategic shift toward software-defined vehicles and AI-native data centers. Major customers include Apple (AAPL +0.22%) and Samsung, and the company recently expanded its reach by acquiring Modular Inc. to diversify its portfolio.
In FY 2025, Qualcomm's revenue reached $44.3 billion, a roughly 13.7% increase over the $39.0 billion reported in FY 2024. Net income for the period, however, fell sharply to $5.5 billion, down about 45% from the $10.1 billion reported in FY 2024, resulting in a net margin of nearly 12.5%, despite the strong top-line growth. The drop in net income wasn't due to weak operations or R&D costs; it was mainly a one-time, non-cash $5.7 billion charge tied to the U.S. government's One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Excluding that charge, Qualcomm's underlying profits actually grew nicely.
As of its September 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio stands at roughly 2.8x, indicating the company has sufficient short-term assets to cover its obligations. The debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.7x, showing a higher level of leverage compared to some peers in the industry. Free cash flow for the fiscal year was nearly $12.8 billion, which is the cash left over after a company pays for its capital expenditures from its operating cash flow.
Advanced Micro Devices faces intense competition from Intel (INTC -3.18%) and Nvidia (NVDA +0.14%), both of which leverage large software ecosystems to maintain market share. Geopolitical tensions also pose a threat, as evidenced by an $800 million inventory charge in early 2025 due to U.S. export controls on sales to China. Additionally, the company relies heavily on third-party foundries like TSMC, making it vulnerable to any manufacturing disruptions or capacity shortages.
Qualcomm deals with significant revenue concentration among a few mobile handset manufacturers, many of whom are increasingly developing their own internal chips. The company also remains highly exposed to regulatory and trade policy risks involving China, which serves as a critical manufacturing hub. Furthermore, ongoing legal challenges to its patent licensing model could fundamentally alter its high-margin revenue streams if future court rulings are unfavorable.
Qualcomm currently trades at a much lower Forward P/E and P/S ratio than AMD, suggesting a more conservative valuation of its future earnings estimates.
Valuation metrics sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.
Which stock would I buy in 2026?
I'd go with AMD, although Qualcomm's ongoing transformation beyond smartphones is worth acknowledging. Its automotive segment just posted a record quarter, growing at an extraordinary rate year over year. A new partnership with BMW cements its position as a key player in next-generation vehicles, and an emerging data center business adds another growth engine that could matter a great deal in the years ahead.
But Qualcomm is also navigating a difficult stretch in its core smartphone business. Android handset demand is soft, and memory cost increases are squeezing margins. A sharp drop in Apple revenue is expected in the coming quarter. Those headwinds are manageable but create near-term uncertainty that concerns me.
The path forward at AMD is considerably cleaner. Data center sales more than doubled year over year. A partnership with Anthropic backs up management's confidence in continued growth, and the company keeps posting results that surprise analysts to the upside. For a long-term investor, AMD's remarkable momentum in the most important part of the semiconductor market makes it the stronger pick right now.

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) Stock Gains on Perplexity AI Collaboration
By Trader EdgeSeptember 25, 2026No Comments3 Mins Read
Shares of AMD gained 2% following the announcement of new AI capabilities developed with Perplexity.
The collaboration integrates Perplexity’s Portable Computer feature into Windows devices running AMD Ryzen AI Max processors.
This integration enables users to execute AI operations locally, eliminating the need to consume Perplexity Computer credits.
The announcement reinforces AMD’s strategic expansion into agentic computing platforms initiated in 2025.
Analysts maintain a Strong Buy consensus on AMD with a mean price target of $648.07.
Shares of Advanced Micro Devices climbed 2% during Friday’s trading session after the semiconductor manufacturer revealed its latest AI integration developed in partnership with Perplexity. The stock’s uptick reflected investor enthusiasm surrounding AMD’s continued advancement in AI-enabled computing devices.
The collaboration focuses on bringing Perplexity’s Portable Computer functionality to Windows-based systems equipped with AMD’s Ryzen AI Max processors, including devices running the Ryzen AI Halo developer platform.
This functionality enables users to perform AI operations entirely on their local hardware. By processing tasks on-device, users can establish automated workflows without depleting their allocation of Perplexity Computer credits used for cloud-based inference.
This development represents the continuation of a multi-year strategy from AMD. The company introduced its inaugural AI-capable PCs in 2023, featuring a dedicated neural processing unit integrated directly into an x86 processor architecture.
The chipmaker accelerated this vision in 2025 by focusing on agentic computing platforms. These systems enable AI agents to operate locally on the device instead of depending exclusively on cloud infrastructure.
AMD executive Jack Huynh addressed the partnership during Wednesday’s announcement. Huynh serves as senior vice president and general manager of the Computing and Graphics Group within AMD.
“We’re entering a new era of computing, where personal AI transforms the PC from a tool into an intelligent partner,” Huynh stated. He emphasized that personal computers are evolving into systems capable of understanding, reasoning, and collaborating with users.
According to Huynh, the Ryzen AI Max processor family enables AI models and intelligent agents to execute directly on personal computers. This architecture provides users the option to process workloads locally while maintaining access to more powerful cloud-based reasoning capabilities when required.
The processor design merges CPU and GPU capabilities with an expansive shared memory architecture. This configuration enables local AI models to operate concurrently with traditional applications without creating performance bottlenecks.
Perplexity contributes its AI model infrastructure and agent technologies to the partnership. The combined offering aims to transform agentic PCs from a specialized novelty into a mainstream computing option.
The strategic importance of this announcement extends beyond the immediate technology. While cloud-based AI processing currently dominates the market, AMD is positioning itself for a potential shift toward local AI execution as user demand evolves.
This strategic positioning explains the positive market response on Friday. Should on-device AI adoption accelerate as AMD anticipates, the company’s early entry into this segment could yield significant competitive advantages.
The Street’s perspective on AMD stock was already positive before this announcement. The consensus rating stands at Strong Buy, supported by 30 Buy recommendations and six Hold ratings issued during the previous three months.
The average analyst price target for AMD stock currently sits at $648.07. Notably, zero Sell ratings have been issued on the stock among tracked analysts.
The Perplexity collaboration provides additional evidence for investors monitoring AMD’s AI PC initiatives. Friday’s stock appreciation demonstrates the market’s immediate response to this strategic development.

Shares of AMD gained 2% following the announcement of new AI capabilities developed with Perplexity.
The collaboration integrates Perplexity’s Portable Computer feature into Windows devices running AMD Ryzen AI Max processors.
This integration enables users to execute AI operations locally, eliminating the need to consume Perplexity Computer credits.
The announcement reinforces AMD’s strategic expansion into agentic computing platforms initiated in 2025.
Analysts maintain a Strong Buy consensus on AMD with a mean price target of $648.07.
Shares of Advanced Micro Devices climbed 2% during Friday’s trading session after the semiconductor manufacturer revealed its latest AI integration developed in partnership with Perplexity. The stock’s uptick reflected investor enthusiasm surrounding AMD’s continued advancement in AI-enabled computing devices.
The collaboration focuses on bringing Perplexity’s Portable Computer functionality to Windows-based systems equipped with AMD’s Ryzen AI Max processors, including devices running the Ryzen AI Halo developer platform.
This functionality enables users to perform AI operations entirely on their local hardware. By processing tasks on-device, users can establish automated workflows without depleting their allocation of Perplexity Computer credits used for cloud-based inference.
This development represents the continuation of a multi-year strategy from AMD. The company introduced its inaugural AI-capable PCs in 2023, featuring a dedicated neural processing unit integrated directly into an x86 processor architecture.
The chipmaker accelerated this vision in 2025 by focusing on agentic computing platforms. These systems enable AI agents to operate locally on the device instead of depending exclusively on cloud infrastructure.
AMD executive Jack Huynh addressed the partnership during Wednesday’s announcement. Huynh serves as senior vice president and general manager of the Computing and Graphics Group within AMD.
“We’re entering a new era of computing, where personal AI transforms the PC from a tool into an intelligent partner,” Huynh stated. He emphasized that personal computers are evolving into systems capable of understanding, reasoning, and collaborating with users.
According to Huynh, the Ryzen AI Max processor family enables AI models and intelligent agents to execute directly on personal computers. This architecture provides users the option to process workloads locally while maintaining access to more powerful cloud-based reasoning capabilities when required.
The processor design merges CPU and GPU capabilities with an expansive shared memory architecture. This configuration enables local AI models to operate concurrently with traditional applications without creating performance bottlenecks.
Perplexity contributes its AI model infrastructure and agent technologies to the partnership. The combined offering aims to transform agentic PCs from a specialized novelty into a mainstream computing option.
The strategic importance of this announcement extends beyond the immediate technology. While cloud-based AI processing currently dominates the market, AMD is positioning itself for a potential shift toward local AI execution as user demand evolves.
This strategic positioning explains the positive market response on Friday. Should on-device AI adoption accelerate as AMD anticipates, the company’s early entry into this segment could yield significant competitive advantages.
The Street’s perspective on AMD stock was already positive before this announcement. The consensus rating stands at Strong Buy, supported by 30 Buy recommendations and six Hold ratings issued during the previous three months.
The average analyst price target for AMD stock currently sits at $648.07. Notably, zero Sell ratings have been issued on the stock among tracked analysts.
The Perplexity collaboration provides additional evidence for investors monitoring AMD’s AI PC initiatives. Friday’s stock appreciation demonstrates the market’s immediate response to this strategic development.
